claims.title: Order details can be modified in transit if shopper transport protection is absent
claims.description: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from the public-internet zone to the internet-facing `process:storefront-api`, but its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` are unknown. If this flow lacks authenticated transport protection and an attacker obtains an on-path position, they can alter order contents, shipping details, or card-last-four before the API processes the request. The altered order can subsequently be forwarded on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` and persisted through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` as a legitimate order record. This is conditional on the unresolved transport attributes, not an assertion that the shopper connection is plaintext.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional: the flow crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to the internet-facing `process:storefront-api`, while protocol and transport encryption are unverified; exploitation also requires an on-path position. Impact is high because altered shopper order data can reach `store:orders-db`, which is confidential and holds `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.summary: Verify authenticated transport for shopper orders
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation on `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`, and record the verified protocol and transport-encryption state in the model.

mitigations.summary: Validate order fields at the receiving API
mitigations.detail: Have `process:storefront-api` canonicalize and allowlist server-acceptable order, shipping, and payment-reference fields before forwarding an order to `process:order-service`.

claims.title: Settlement status can be modified in transit if webhook transport protection is absent
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` is a public-internet-to-DMZ boundary crossing whose protocol and `encryption_in_transit` are unknown. If the webhook lacks authenticated transport protection and an attacker gains an on-path position, they can alter a settlement confirmation before `process:storefront-api` marks an order paid. The modification changes financial order state at the internet-facing settlement receiver; this is conditional on the unverified transport attributes, rather than a claim that the processor webhook is plaintext.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because this is a public-internet boundary crossing with unverified protocol and transport encryption, although an attacker must also obtain an on-path position. Impact is medium because the callback controls whether an order is treated as paid and the flow is tagged `financial`.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated TLS for the settlement webhook
mitigations.detail: Use HTTPS with strict certificate validation for `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`, and record the confirmed protocol and encryption state.

mitigations.summary: Bind settlement callbacks to expected transactions
mitigations.detail: Require the receiver to validate signed callback contents against the expected processor transaction and order state before marking an order paid.

claims.title: Forged settlement callbacks can mark orders paid if webhook authentication is absent
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` accepts a write-shaped settlement callback from the third-party `entity:card-processor`, but its authentication state is unknown. If the unresolved callback authentication does not include processor signature verification or equivalent sender authentication, an outside attacker can submit a fabricated settlement confirmation to `process:storefront-api` and cause an order to be treated as paid. This is conditional on the unknown authentication attribute; the source explicitly says that callback authentication still needs to be checked.

quotes.text: I would have to check how that callback is authenticated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown webhook authentication: `process:storefront-api` is internet-facing and the callback crosses from `boundary:public-internet`, so an outside party can attempt delivery if no sender verification exists. Impact is medium because a forged callback changes financial settlement state for an order.

mitigations.detail: Require `process:storefront-api` to verify a processor-specific webhook signature using a protected secret or public key before accepting a settlement update.
Bind each callback to an expected processor transaction, enforce timestamp and nonce or event-ID replay protection, and permit only valid payment-state transitions.

claims.title: Orders can be injected into the core service by any reachable caller
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` has authentication stated absent, and the source says `process:order-service` accepts anything that can reach it. An attacker who first gains execution in `process:storefront-api` or another foothold able to reach the core service can inject fabricated or modified order submissions directly to `process:order-service`, bypassing the storefront's normal session handling. The order service can then persist the attacker-controlled order through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`; this is a stated absent-control finding, not a claim that the internal service is internet-exposed.

quotes.text: There is no auth on that gRPC call — the order service accepts anything that can reach it

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: the attacker needs a foothold that can reach the internal `process:order-service`, but no authentication is required once reachable. Impact is high because injected orders can be written to confidential `store:orders-db`, which holds `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.summary: Require service-to-service authentication for order submission
mitigations.detail: Configure mTLS or workload identity so `process:order-service` accepts `submit-order` only from the authorized `process:storefront-api` identity.

mitigations.summary: Authorize and validate each submitted order
mitigations.detail: Make `process:order-service` verify the caller identity and enforce server-side order-state, amount, and shopper-ownership validation before writing `store:orders-db`.

claims.title: Order instructions can be modified on the DMZ-to-core gRPC path if transport integrity is absent
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services`; its `encryption_in_transit` state is unknown, while authentication is explicitly absent. If this gRPC hop lacks authenticated transport protection and an attacker obtains a position on the DMZ-to-core path, they can rewrite order contents or shopper identifiers before `process:order-service` captures them. The altered data can be committed through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`, turning an in-flight modification into an authoritative order record. This remains conditional on the unknown transport-encryption state and does not infer a path position merely from that unknown.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional: the flow is a decided DMZ-to-core crossing with transport encryption unverified, but exploitation requires a foothold on that path. Impact is high because altered orders are processed by `process:order-service` and can corrupt confidential `store:orders-db` records holding `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.summary: Use mutually authenticated TLS for the gRPC hop
mitigations.detail: Require mTLS with verified service identities and authenticated encryption on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order`.

mitigations.summary: Detect instruction modification at the receiver
mitigations.detail: Have `process:order-service` validate a signed or integrity-bound order envelope from `process:storefront-api` before accepting it for capture.

claims.title: A stolen application-account password permits direct alteration of all order records
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` uses one application account with full read/write authority, and its password is kept in an environment variable on `process:order-service`. An attacker who recovers that static credential from a compromised worker, image, log, or runtime environment can alter rows directly in `store:orders-db`, bypassing the validation performed by `process:order-service`. The corruption reaches every consumer that reads order data through the same read-write flow, including future order and receipt processing; the model does not describe an independent reconciliation path that would reject altered records.

quotes.text: the order service reads and writes with a single application account that has full read/write. The password comes from an environment variable on the worker.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because an attacker must first recover the application-account password or compromise `process:order-service`, but the credential is static and held in that worker's environment. Impact is high because the account has full read/write authority over confidential `store:orders-db`, which contains `pii` and `financial` order data.

mitigations.summary: Replace the static database password with workload identity
mitigations.detail: Use short-lived workload-federated database credentials for `process:order-service` rather than an application password stored in an environment variable.
Restrict the application principal to the minimum tables and statements required for order capture, and separate read and write roles where possible.

claims.title: Offline alteration of orders-db media is possible if at-rest integrity protection is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` holds confidential shopper-address, card-last-four, and order data, but its `encryption_at_rest` state is unknown. If copies of its media, snapshots, or storage are not protected by encryption with integrity verification and an attacker obtains such a copy, they can alter stored order records before the data is restored or otherwise accepted by the database. The resulting corruption is consumed by `process:order-service` through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`. This is conditional on the unknown at-rest protection and does not assert that an unencrypted backup exists.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the attacker must obtain a storage copy, while `store:orders-db` at-rest encryption is unverified. Impact is high because the store is classified confidential and holds `pii` and `financial` data whose integrity is used by `process:order-service`.

mitigations.summary: Verify protected storage for database media and backups
mitigations.detail: Use managed envelope encryption with authenticated integrity protection for `store:orders-db`, including snapshots and backups, and record the confirmed at-rest control.
Require integrity-checked, authorized restore procedures and reconcile restored order records before returning the database to service.

claims.title: Receipt archive integrity is unresolved because the model and source disagree on storage protection
claims.description: `store:receipt-archive` holds business-critical receipt records, while the model states `encryption_at_rest` is absent but the submitted source states that the bucket uses a customer-managed key; the evidence catalog records this as a disagreement. Until the actual storage and restore integrity controls are verified, an attacker holding a storage copy could alter receipt objects and have a modified receipt later treated as an authentic completed-order record. The affected record can be consumed by systems that rely on `store:receipt-archive`; no independent validation or restore-integrity check is modeled. This is a conditional finding driven by the control discrepancy, not a claim that the source-stated customer-managed key is absent.

quotes.text: the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the attacker must first obtain a storage copy and the source states a customer-managed key, although the catalog identifies a disagreement that must be resolved. Impact is medium because `store:receipt-archive` contains `business-critical-data` and altered receipts can undermine the integrity of completed-order records.

mitigations.summary: Resolve and document the receipt archive protection state
mitigations.detail: Reconcile the model's absent `encryption_at_rest` value with the source-stated customer-managed key and document whether bucket objects, versions, backups, and restores receive authenticated integrity protection.

mitigations.summary: Protect receipt writes and validate receipt integrity
mitigations.detail: Use object versioning and retention controls, restrict write and restore authority, and store or verify an application-level receipt signature before relying on a receipt as a completed-order record.
